title: the transporter (Star Trek)
stem: The teleporter is totally safe — millions of trips, zero accidents, the technician doesn't even look up anymore. It scans you, builds a perfect copy of you at your destination, and the you standing on the pad is gone, painlessly, in the same instant. Do you step on?

opts.t: Energize. The pattern is the person; sentiment about which atoms is exactly that — sentiment.
Never. What steps off is a *second thing*. Where a thing has actually been matters, even if no scanner could ever tell the difference. I'll take the shuttle.
One question first, and the manual can't answer it: what will *I* experience? Not the me who waves from the far pad — me. Nobody answers that in the third person.
To everyone at the destination, that's me — completely. To this room, something ends. Both are the case, and there is no extra fact about which one is 'really' me. I'd step on.
It moves millions a day and the technician is bored. What happens 'during' is a question for people with too much layover.
Before I board I want the incident report — the famous one, where the pad glitched and *two* walked away. What they did next tells you what this machine actually is.
The manifest already knows whether I arrive. I'll find out at the gate.
The scanner gets every atom and misses the passenger. Something looks out of these eyes, and it isn't in the schematic.

title: the coincidence (11:11)
stem: You think of an old friend for the first time in years. That same evening, they text you. What just happened?

opts.t: Count the times you thought of someone and nothing happened. Nobody logs the misses. That's what just happened.
It's been like this all week — their initials, that song, 11:11. I don't have to explain it to notice it.
A coincidence — but a useful one: it told me I miss them. I'd answer fast either way.
A text arrived. That's the entire event.
For me it's uncanny; for them it's Tuesday. Both descriptions are complete.
Given enough friends and enough evenings, the real surprise would be this *never* happening.
The thought and the text share a cause somewhere upstream. Things that meet were aimed.

title: the train (Sliding Doors)
stem: A canceled meeting puts you on an earlier train than usual. You end up next to an old acquaintance who starts gossiping — no idea you know the people involved. Mid-story, you realize you now know something you were never meant to: years ago, before things got serious, your best friend's partner cheated. Once. They're happy now. What do you do?

opts.t: Tell. The truth doesn't expire, and my friend is navigating their life with a wrong map. Painful beats false.
Nothing. The relationship in front of me works; excavating what's underneath it answers no question anyone is asking.
What happened was one thing inside their relationship and another from where I stand. I don't hold their fact — I hold a stranger's copy of it. Not mine to install.
Telling isn't handing them a fact — it's forcing a bet they never placed. I'd sit with my friend, learn what they'd *want* to know, before deciding I know it for them.
The unbearable option is knowing forever and saying nothing. I go to the partner: you tell them, or I do. Either way it resolves.
I make the rule that the version of me who missed this train could also endorse — what should *anyone* do with this, every time — then I do that, even when it stings.
A canceled meeting, that seat, that stranger, that story. By the time a train has handed you a thing like this, what you'll do with it was already aboard. I'll watch myself find out.
I wasn't meant to catch that train — or I was. Information doesn't ride to you for nothing. I'd wait until it's clear why it came to me.

title: the cut to black (Inception / Sopranos)
stem: A movie ends by cutting to black right before you find out the answer. Walking out, you and your friends are already arguing about what really happened — and mid-sentence you realize this one can never be settled. The answer just isn't in the movie. Where do you land?

opts.t: Then the director owes us. Somebody knows what the script said; there are interviews; there is an on-record answer and I will find it or die cranky.
The frame exists — it existed *on set*. Continuity notes, props, what the actors were told that morning. The answer is in the world even if it isn't in the film.
The cut is the answer: the film ends exactly where the question stops being the film's business. Respect it.
The film you watched and the film I watched ended differently. Two tickets, two films. Nothing needs reconciling in the lobby.
The ending is whatever each viewer walked in carrying. That's not a cop-out — that's what endings are for.
Both endings are in that cut. That's what the cut *is*. The film is complete — it's just bigger than one screening of it.
The film was always going to end there, and you were always going to need it not to. Enjoy the drive home.
I don't think it's an accident which ending each person needs it to be. The film shows you yours.

title: the album (palate cleanser; plays at slot 5)

opts.t: Discovery — Daft Punk. Every single sound on it came from somewhere, and people have found them all. That's what makes it *better*.
The Smile Sessions — Beach Boys. The 'finished' album never came out, and it doesn't need to. Every version is the album.
Blonde — Frank Ocean. Memories bent to how they felt instead of how they happened — which is the honest version.
ABBA Gold. Not technically an album, and I will not be taking questions.
Unknown Pleasures — Joy Division. The cover is literally a chart of pulsar data. Austere. Measurable. No notes wasted.

4'33" — John Cage. Nobody plays a note, and it still comes out exactly as it was always going to — four and a half minutes of the world proceeding without anyone's input. Every performance goes perfectly.
The Dark Side of the Moon — started at the exact moment the lion roars the third time. It syncs. It syncs *too well*. Explain that.
The Grey Album — Danger Mouse. It's just two other records meeting each other. It was never even officially released — and it's still completely real.

title: the 3am replay (La La Land epilogue / EEAAO)
stem: It's 3am and you're replaying a decision from last year that went badly. What are you actually replaying?

opts.t: The information I had at the time. Given that, I'd bet the same way again — the outcome was bad, the bet was fine. Filed, updated, closed.
The detail I missed. It was there, it was findable — that's the part that stings and the part that teaches.
The whole other life, playing out in montage — where they'd be by now, who they'd know, the apartment. I can visit. I just can't stay.
The exact moment it tipped. Everything before that was recoverable; I want to know precisely where it stopped being.
Nothing, honestly. I don't do replays — it happened, it's over, there's nothing back there to watch.
Depends who's asking. The version I tell my mother, my partner, and myself at 3am are three different calls — none of them the original.
'The call' — as if there were a fork. There was a person, being exactly who they were, doing the only thing that person does. I've stopped grading it.
It went badly so that something else could happen. I've started looking for what.

title: the magician's offer (The Prestige)
stem: A magician fools you so badly you lose sleep over it. A week later you run into them, and they offer to tell you how the trick was done — with a warning: knowing ruins it. Do you want to know?

opts.t: Instantly. The explanation is the best part; a mystery is just a mechanism I haven't met yet. Nothing true gets worse by being known.
No. For one moment the world was something other than solid and ordinary, and that moment is worth protecting from the truth. Keep your secret.
No, and not out of romance: the trick works whether or not I know how. Knowing adds nothing I can use.
Yes — but what I actually want explained is the other half of the trick: me, being fooled. That mechanism I can take home.
Yes, and then the general theory — not this trick, all tricks. One principle, every card.
Yes, and then let me try it until it breaks on me. You only understand a trick at the edge where it fails.
The trick I'd be told isn't the trick the person beside me saw. There were as many tricks as seats.
Take it or don't — I was always going to be fooled, and knowing how won't make the next one avoidable.

title: the 30% wedding (forecast discourse)
stem: Your friend's outdoor wedding. The weather app said 30% chance of rain. It poured from the first speech to the last dance. Was the app wrong?

opts.t: No. A 30% isn't a promise, it's a posture. The forecast did its job; the sky did its thing.
That's my real complaint: said that way, it can never be caught being wrong. Show me their track record — if their 30%s come true about three times in ten, I'll forgive any one Saturday.
Yes — not as a bet, as a description. That storm was already assembled off the coast by morning. Someone with better data knew.
'Wrong' isn't a property forecasts have. It said 30, it rained, the marquee was cheap insurance nobody bought.
The 30 was right about the whole population of Saturdays like that one. This particular soaked wedding isn't evidence about anything.
Wrong for the bride, fine for the region, excellent for the reservoir. 'The forecast' was never one thing.
The rain, the app, and everyone's decision to trust it were never separate things. There's nothing to blame — it all arrived together.
It rained on the one day it mattered, on the one hour it mattered most. At some point 'chance' stops being the humble explanation.

title: morning pages (The Artist's Way)
stem: Say you keep a journal with one strict rule: write every morning, never read it back. Nobody else will ever read it either. Is the writing actually doing anything?

opts.t: Everything. The reader was never the point; the writing rearranges the *writer*. It's the most honest instrument I own.
Something happens between me and the page, every morning. That it goes no further doesn't make it less — most of what happens goes no further.
It's doing what everything does: existing. The pages are real, the ink is real; readership was always a separate question.
If no one ever reads it, then whether it's 'doing anything' is a question with no consequences either way. But you keep showing up every morning — so it's doing that.
Yes — and the rule is the whole point. I don't need to read them for the pages to count; I need the practice to be total. No exceptions, no peeking, no special mornings.
No — and I'd stop. Output nothing can ever check isn't reflection, it's rehearsal. Say one sentence out loud to a real person instead.
A day fully attended to is different afterward, and so is the person attending. Attention is never wasted — it goes somewhere.

title: two cities (Moneyball / the pro-con list)
stem: You're choosing between two cities — basically two different lives. You make the spreadsheet: pros, cons, weights, the works. It picks the city you don't want. What now?

opts.t: I go with the spreadsheet. I built it precisely because I knew this moment would come, and gut-me doesn't get a veto it didn't earn.
I open the formulas. The dread means an input is wrong — the gut is usually reporting something it can't cite yet.
The dread *is* data — a criterion I was too embarrassed to weight. Back into the model it goes, honestly this time.
Spreadsheets are for narrowing, not deciding. It did its job; now I do mine.
A month there, sublet, cheap flights — run the trial the scouts in my head keep scoffing at. Arguments end; seasons conclude.
I show it to three friends and get three verdicts on 'what it says.' The spreadsheet was never going to be the last conversation.
The spreadsheet, the gut, and the eventual choice are one process pretending to be three. I watch it finish.
I notice which cell my eye keeps snagging on. The discomfort is pointing somewhere; numbers are one of the ways it talks.
